The DevOps agent: the through-line story

The running example is an autonomous DevOps agent for hundreds of microservices, chosen because all five flaws appear there daily. Initial state, 3:47 a.m.: PagerDuty pages “High latency on checkout-service.” The SRE hops Grafana (a spike, not a why) → Datadog (pool saturated) → Splunk (errors from stripe-python, updated two hours prior) → CI/CD history: 45 minutes of diagnosis, a 5-minute fix — the new stripe-python had changed connection-pooling behavior and exhausted database connections. The state is fragmented monitoring, the SRE as reasoning engine, reactive response — “The initial state is a representation problem, not a technology problem… There is no graph. There are only strings.” The arc: Ch. 3 a queryable digital twin; Ch. 4 bitemporal memory; Ch. 5 a diagnostician that builds its own workflow graph; Ch. 6 hands via MCP; Ch. 7 self-healing — a routine stripe-python 3.2.1 → 3.3.0 change is partially predicted (right pathway, wrong mechanism), fixed by cognitive autopsy + semantic backpropagation; Ch. 8 selective intelligence and governance — deployment events end to end in under 2 seconds, ~$0.002 per event. Corroboration: AnyShift runs production graph-based DevOps agents on ~100 handcrafted relationship types, per-node historical queues, AWS + Terraform/IaC, event-driven updates.

Project status Dual-graph split in place; harness surfaces 1–6 stubbed; the diagnosis DAG runs against the KG. Next: populate the vertical graph properly (Ch. 3).

Takeaways

  • Dual graph: vertical KG = what it knows, horizontal workflow graph = how it acts — the map and the route.
  • The harness’s six surfaces + promise theory: harness design sets the upper bound; model swaps bounded, harness swaps unbounded.
  • Split nodes by tool surface, not prompt (RedAI; >80% overlap → merge).
  • Context graph = reification + bitemporal metadata + decision traces; the book keeps “vertical knowledge graph.”
  • Eight pillars map one-to-one onto the five flaws (Table 2-1); layered, not independent.
  • DevOps storyline: 45 min at 3:47 a.m. → <2 s at ~$0.002; the 3.2.1→3.3.0 partial prediction is Ch. 7’s hinge.

Chapter 3

Graph-Based Knowledge Modeling for Agentic Systems

≈ 6 minfour-stage framework · three-graph architecture · OWA/CWA · reification · entity resolution

Knowledge representation is the engine of agentic systems — relational stores, document stores, embeddings all fragment knowledge with no native relationship awareness. Hence the reframe: “the flow of intelligence must be reversed” — use AI to restructure fragmented organizational knowledge into a machine-comprehensible semantic foundation. Zhou et al. (2026) supply the orienting four-stage framework: graph building → index construction → operator configuration → retrieval and generation.

Build vs buy — and what buying never includes

Decide on six criteria: control and flexibility, performance and scale, operational complexity, integration flexibility, cost, use case. Managed: Neo4j, TigerGraph, Amazon Neptune, FalkorDB; custom: PostgreSQL + Apache AGE, MongoDB — start managed to validate modeling, go custom for schema-evolution control and hybrid vector reasoning. Buying never includes the domain schema, reasoning patterns, integration logic, or ontology scope — just the engine, the query language (Cypher, GSQL, SPARQL), and tooling.

Start from reasoning requirements — three models, scored on five features:

The reasoning–representation trade-off — the book’s five evaluation features.
FeatureLPGRDFHypergraph
Formal reasoningAd hocStrongest (native inference)Structural
N-ary relationsRelation nodesNeeds reificationNatural (hyperedges)
PerformanceBest traversalSlow at scaleModerate
Tool ecosystemRich (Neo4j, Neptune, ArangoDB)FragmentedImmature
Constraint expressivenessLimited (SHACL validates)OWL infers; SHACL rejectsLimited

The hyperedge prescription is the book’s worked example: HyperEdge(type="Prescription", nodes={doctor, patient, medication, dosage, date, condition}) — one edge, six participants. A PostgreSQL triples table with confidence columns suffices for predictable retrieval; dedicated graphs win for temporal reasoning, contradiction management, incremental processing. Across the spectrum — passage graphs, trees, knowledge graphs, textual and rich knowledge graphs — most agentic systems land on some form of KG.

Open-world vs closed-world is an agent-safety axis

RDF assumes the OWA: an absent fact is unknown; relational databases and most LPG tooling assume the CWA: absence means negation. Agents are the first consumers that reason from absence — “does this patient have a contraindication?” OWA answers “unknown,” CWA answers “no.” Cagle (2026) shows SPARQL’s OPTIONAL+FILTER silently applying CWA semantics to OWA data, and named graphs acting as implicit CWA scopes.

Hence three SHACL shape patterns: pre-retrieval shapes (queried entities: a Service needs :owningTeam, :deploymentTarget, recent :dependencyStatusTimestamp), pre-action shapes (tool preconditions: RollbackDeployment requires :rollbackApproved true + :lastKnownGoodVersion), post-write shapes (agent writes validated pre-commit: CAUSED_BY needs endpoints and provenance). OWL infers; SHACL rejects. Tip: SHACL is mandatory for read/write agents; never gate on OPTIONAL+FILTER — use ASK + SHACL prevalidation; record the OWA/CWA stance per named graph (domain OWA, lexical CWA, subject mixed).

The three-graph architecture

The centerpiece separates knowledge by origin, certainty, and semantic role. The domain graph: trusted, curated, entity-resolved data with stable identifiers. The lexical graph: raw text — document and chunk nodes with embeddings, immutable, fully provenanced; it provides the “retrieval” in RAG. The subject graph: LLM-extracted facts as interpretation artifacts with confidence, model versions, timestamps. Merging directly causes unverified pollution, lost provenance, cascading extraction errors, unverifiable reasoning. Entity resolution bridges subject → domain via CORRESPONDS_TO edges above similarity thresholds; EXTRACTED_FROM links subject → lexical, so product → reported issues → verbatim review text traversals yield aggregated evidence with provenance. Deploy physically, logically (labels :Product vs :Subject_Product), or via namespacing; re-extract the subject graph as models improve — the domain graph never moves. Multimodal: canonical entities carry modality; per-modality embeddings share one unified space (Gemini Embedding 2 — cross-modal retrieval = one ANN query); typed cross-modal edges (image_depicts, table_specifies) live in the subject graph.

Schema patterns are reification — and a safety mechanism

All four design patterns promote an edge or property into a first-class node so metadata, provenance, and temporal bounds can attach — the hallmark of a context graph. Event-centric: Meeting nodes with hasParticipant/hasPrecedingEvent edges; DevOps deployments become events (create_deployment_event: DEPLOYS → Service, MODIFIES → Compute). Contextual boundary: a Context node (Project-X, validDuring 2023-01-01→06-30) prevents mixing information across domains or time. Multiperspective: contradiction as structure — Revenue-Forecast 10M according-to Finance (0.8) vs 12M according-to Sales (0.7); configuration drift becomes Terraform-vs-cloud perspectives rather than an error. Capability model: the agent’s limits as queryable nodes — Process-Refund requires Financial-System-Access, a Supervisor, and a 500-USD limit; a $600 request → escalation. Patterns combine.

💡 Key idea

Homoiconic representation — code and data share one representation. Metaknowledge structures (a metaschema describing the schema itself; EntityType "Person" stored as data) let agents inspect and modify their own ontology. Executable patterns store rules as data — Rule "DetermineCustomerSegment": a Cypher purchase count; Premium >20, Regular >10, else Basic — queryable, explainable, modifiable: the on-ramp to self-modification (Ch. 5, 7).

Ontologies as the agent instruction manual

The organization spectrum runs pick lists → taxonomies → thesauruses → ontologies. An ontology has five components — classes, subclasses, individuals, axioms, relationships (healthcare: Person→Patient/Oncologist; ≤1 primary physician). SKOS bridges vocabularies (skos:exactMatch/broader/related) so automobile/car/vehicle don’t fragment; upper ontologies (BFO, DOLCE) anchor integration (:Person rdfs:subClassOf bfo:Object); merging uses four techniques — class hierarchy alignment, property alignment, instance matching, axiom harmonization. The distinctive move is behavioral annotation: properties marked identifying (Artist.artist_name), relationships contextualizing (CREATED) or noncontextualizing (BROADER) — an agent hitting “Andy Warhol” as Artist or Subject can ask the ontology what identifies the entity. Ontology plus ER have moved from back-office MDM to core platform capability — “30 AI agents in a day — now what?” The ontology is their playbook.

Entity resolution: evidence, not vibes

LLM matching is generalization-based — statistical regularities, nondeterministic, miscalibrated, weak on non-Western names. Evidence-based ER (Senzing’s school) computes specific features plus domain rules with honest confidence: “89% confidence because NAME matched 87%, ADDRESS 100%, PHONE 95%.” Forrester’s 2025 TEI of Senzing: payback under 6 months, 226% ROI over three years, 95% reduction in time to add new data sources. Adversaries exploit channel separation (Bob Smith / Bob R. Smith II / Robert Smith Jr.); channel consolidation is the answer — calibrated by cases like John R Smith ≠ John E Smith (one letter; don’t merge without evidence). ER yields the graph’s building blocks: entities with stable identifiers, typed relations (RESOLVED, POSSIBLY_RELATED, DISCLOSED), aggregated properties, per-match evidence metadata — explainable AI by construction.

Extraction frameworks

For LLM-based construction: iText2KG (incremental, topic-independent, schema-agnostic; disambiguation at ent_threshold=0.8; now enhanced into ATOM); RAKG (retrieval-augmented construction; ~96% accuracy, 88% entity coverage, 95% relationship fidelity); ATOM (Lairgi, 2026) attacks the LLM “forgetting effect” with atomic facts (<400-token chunks keep exhaustivity >0.8), parallel 5-tuple extraction (subject, predicate, object, t_start, t_end) with dual-time modeling, O(log N) merging — on COVID-19 corpora: +31% factual exhaustivity, +18% temporal, +17% stability, −93% latency. Multi-agent construction favors the proposer-approver pattern (intent → discovery → schema proposal with critic → deterministic construction, human gates). Entity linking is three-stage: property-key correlation → value similarity (Jaro-Winkler; 0.95/0.85/0.75 by stakes) → context-aware validation, targeting >75% link rate, >0.85 confidence, <5% ambiguity.

DevOps capstone: the digital twin

The capstone (inspired by AnyShift) reconciles AWS/GCP/Azure, Kubernetes, Terraform, Git, and observability into a time-versioned KG. Context engineering in one line: without graph context LLMs hallucinate vpc-123abc; with it they emit data.terraform_remote_state.vpc.outputs.vpc_id. A canonical multi-cloud ontology abstracts provider noise — compute, networking, storage, access-control, service, operational entities — related by DEPENDS_ON, ROUTES_TO, ASSUMES_ROLE, OWNED_BY, PART_OF, DEPLOYED_BY, LINKS_TO. Observability becomes structure (Monitor and LogSource nodes): the graph answers what/how, external systems answer how much/what happened. Three showcase queries: dependencies (DEPENDS_ON*1..4), drift (Terraform vs AWS API, WHERE tf.value <> cloud.value), impact (VPC → services → 99.99% SLAs → teams). Infrastructure ER resolves one EC2 instance behind i-abc123, an IP, a DNS name, a Terraform name (vector search at 0.85, confirmed by relationship patterns). Quality is instrumented on four dimensions:

The four context-quality metrics — instrument from day one; Chapter 7 consumes them.
MetricDefinitionBook’s example
PrecisionSample edges vs live APIs<0.95 means drift
ExhaustivenessEntities found vs actual247 EC2 vs 198 Compute nodes = 20% blind spots
FreshnessAge of ingested statealert >1 hour stale in production
CoverageRelationship types present vs defined8 present of 15 defined
Project status Canonical ontology + three-graph separation live; stripe-python 3.2.1 and its Terraform definitions now resolve to one entity. Next: give the twin a memory (Ch. 4).

Takeaways

  • Three-graph architecture — domain/lexical/subject — linked by CORRESPONDS_TO/EXTRACTED_FROM; entity resolution is the connective operation.
  • OWA vs CWA is an agent-safety axis; three SHACL patterns (pre-retrieval, pre-action, post-write); never OPTIONAL+FILTER.
  • Four reification patterns: event-centric, contextual boundary, multiperspective, capability model — drift and authority limits become structure.
  • Evidence-based ER: honest confidence (89% = NAME 87 + ADDRESS 100 + PHONE 95); RESOLVED/POSSIBLY_RELATED/DISCLOSED.
  • Extraction: iText2KG / RAKG / ATOM (atomic 5-tuples, dual-time); proposer-approver; three-stage linking.
  • Homoiconicity — metaknowledge + executable rules — makes the ontology agent-modifiable.

Chapter 4

Agentic Graph Memory Systems

≈ 6 minGit for knowledge · four memory operations · Letta/A-Mem/Graphiti · Cognee/mem0/Zep · MEM1

An agent ships; users are thrilled for a week; then: “Why doesn’t it remember me?” The memory implementation is fundamentally broken — and the Letta Leaderboard catalogues eight co-occurring failure modes: missing already-available information; broken hierarchies (trivia in prime memory, critical facts archived); key information missed even when present; retrieval degrading with volume; new overwriting old so change can’t be explained; silos blocking cross-reference; blurring timelines; works at hundreds of facts, collapses at thousands. Bigger windows don’t rescue it — a million tokens fills fast, and recursive language models (Zhang, 2025) show context rot well before hard limits. The killer diagnosis: externalization without version control makes failures impossible to audit; concurrent agent writes reduce to last-write-wins with no conflict record.

Git for knowledge

The prescription: treat agentic memory like a Git repository — version every ontological commit, agents branch while processing and merge when finished, CI checks before accepting changes. Schema drift becomes visible and reversible; merge conflicts surface contradictions (“Document A says Maria won; Document B says Camille won”). Three memory consistency models govern concurrency: eventual (converge eventually — research literature reviews), strong (synchronous barrier per write — mandatory when one agent finds a drug interaction others must see before treating), causal (causally related updates in order — the practical middle). Git mapping: PR review = strong, CI on branches = eventual, dependency-ordered merge queue = causal. Default causal; strong only for irreversible actions.

Computer architecture for memory

Borrowing from hardware: an I/O layer of raw inputs and tool outputs (ephemeral, write-heavy, read-once); a cache layer of active reasoning context — a bounded subgraph feeding the context window, “the scarcest resource in any agentic system”; and a persistent layer of full history with temporal versioning, branching, merging — the only layer that survives sessions. Vendors: Cognee persists, mem0 caches, Zep does both, Letta puts the cache-to-persistent boundary under agent control — “agentic memory management.” Convergence: “memory is not a log; it is a graph that evolves over time.”

The building blocks: MemoryNode (stable identity — update “John from marketing,” don’t duplicate; content, type, timestamps, embedding, extensible metadata) and typed, time-bounded, weighted edges. Latimer et al. 2025 (Hindsight is 20/20) adds four epistemic networks — World (objective external facts), Experience (the agent’s own actions), Opinion (beliefs with confidence), Observation (synthesized entity summaries) — so “developers and users can see what the agent knows versus what it believes.” Zep organizes memory as three subgraph tiers — episode (raw interactions, append-only), semantic entity (deduplicated, enriched), community (rebuilt clusters) — with inter-tier edges keeping beliefs traceable to raw interactions. Graphiti supplies the bitemporal core: validity window + ingestion timeline on every edge — TemporalEdge(valid_from, valid_until, ingested_at, invalidation_reason), invalidate(reason), was_valid_at(ts) — “from a static snapshot into a movie you can pause, rewind, and inspect.” Hindsight weights typed links so causal/entity connections (μ > 1) outrank weak semantic ones during spreading activation.

The four essential memory operations

  1. Consolidating — the “sleep” phase: cluster by similarity, summarize, create consolidated memories with provenance chains. Sleep-time compute (Letta + UC Berkeley, Lin et al. 2025) cuts active inference costs 5× and adds 13–18% accuracy at equal budget — run in idle periods, never in the response path.
  2. Indexing — four layered types: semantic, keyword, temporal, relational — a latency alert pulls similar incidents, narrows to last week, walks to upstream dependencies.
  3. Updating — mark old facts superseded/deprecated, link old↔new via versioned nodes and explicit supersedes edges. Never delete.
  4. Retrieving — “intelligent context assembly under uncertainty”: all four channels in parallel, merged via reciprocal rank fusion (rank-based, no calibration), reranked by a neural cross-encoder, filtered to the token budget — “a slice of the agent’s entire memory.”

Granularity: fragments lose cross-turn context; Hindsight extracts two to five comprehensive narrative facts per conversation. And a 10-participant meeting needs 45 pairwise edges — hence hypergraphs, the HyperEdge first-class and indexed by type, time, participant.

Three production patterns, three platform profiles

Letta (MemGPT) hierarchical memory (Packer et al., 2024): recall_memory (raw history), core_memory (highest-value facts, core_limit=2000 as a forcing function), archival_memory (unlimited, slower); extract_key_facts promotes durable attributes (“allergic to peanuts”) over states (“having coffee now”); a full core evicts by usage, not FIFO — “eviction is not deletion.” A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025) models how new facts change what you know — each relationship an update, refinement, contradiction, or new branch, then evolve_connected_memories marks “Sarah’s previous role” historical. Graphiti (Rasmussen et al., 2025) does everything incrementally: extract entities from new content only, resolve them (“the marketing director” → existing Sarah node), update only the impacted neighborhood — sub-second at millions of nodes.

As reference architectures: Cognee is graph-first (ECL = Extract / Cognify / Load; 30+ sources; Dynamo.fyi +16% answer relevancy; trade-off: ontology literacy). mem0 is selective-hybrid (vector + graph + key-value; two-phase add/update/discard; ~10% permanent retention, dodging the “junk drawer problem”; ~90% token savings, LOCOMO 66.9% vs OpenAI’s 52.9%; browser extension attaches memory to the user across vendors; trade-off: shallower relationships). Zep is bitemporal and explainable (P95 ≈ 300 ms via precomputed artifacts; clustering ≈ logarithmic search; invalidation as expiration with history preserved; ~94.8% Deep Memory Retrieval). Combinable — Cognee for relationships, mem0 for simplicity and cost, Zep for temporal reasoning and auditability.

Training agents to use memory: MEM1

LLMs can’t decide what’s worth remembering, create-vs-update, or retrieval-benefit vs context-pollution — the graph becomes “a digital hoarder’s attic.” MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2025) makes memory a behavior learned by RL: Phase 1, task-oriented learning with task rewards; Phase 2, consolidation through constraints — a memory budget (budget=1000 → consolidate_or_fail()) forces trade-offs; “the constraint… is part of the training signal”; Phase 3, multi-objective mastery (accuracy + latency, then satisfaction, cost, safety). Results: agents distinguish importance without heuristics, consolidation strategies emerge from task demands, and 7B models with learned memory behavior outperformed 70B models with hand-engineered policies. Reward task success, never memory perfection; mask training signals per module. “Dynamic memory without dynamic schemas”: the consolidated state itself becomes a learned schema.

🧭 Book framework

Six operational health metrics: node growth rate, edge density (watch hubs), cluster balance, query latency (P95/P99 per query type), memory conflicts, temporal consistency (“a deployment must precede the errors it causes”). Wire them to automated maintenance and the memory starts healing itself.

DevOps capstone: incident memory

The digital twin gains a memory: EPISODE_TYPES = ["Incident","Deployment","ConfigChange","Alert","Conversation"], TEMPORAL_EDGES = ["PRECEDED_BY","CAUSED_BY","CORRELATED_WITH","SUPERSEDES"], KNOWLEDGE_TYPES = ["Pattern","Preference","Runbook","RiskFactor"]. ingest_episode embeds, links affected entities, and chains preceding episodes within a 24-hour window; the root-cause query find_changes_before_incident(incident_id, lookback_hours=4) scores candidates by time proximity and causal strength; consolidate() skips clusters under 3 episodes, finds common precursors, and creates patterns with DERIVED_FROM provenance. RL comes via Amazon Nova Forge “bring your own orchestration”: a DevOpsMemoryEnvironment with store/retrieve/consolidate/forget actions, memory budget 1,000 nodes (over → reward −1.0), reward = evaluate_incident_resolution() — incident resolution, not memory operations. Four behaviors emerge from reward alone: selective storage, multistage retrieval (broad → narrow → causal expansion), adaptive consolidation timing, strategic forgetting. Future-proofing: neurosymbolic integration (Garcez and Lamb, 2020), distributed sharding, continual precomputation. “Facts are cheap; the connections between them are where the intelligence emerges.”

Project status The twin remembers: bitemporal DEPENDS_ON history survives the 3.2.1→3.3.0 upgrade; find_changes_before_incident returns the upgrade as top candidate. Next: reason over it (Ch. 5).

Takeaways

  • Memory like Git: versioned commits, branching/merging agents, CI checks; default causal consistency, strong only for irreversible actions.
  • Four operations: consolidation (sleep-time compute), indexing (semantic/keyword/temporal/relational), supersede-don’t-delete, RRF-fused retrieval + cross-encoder + token budget.
  • I/O / cache / persistent layers; Zep’s episode/entity/community tiers; Hindsight’s world/experience/opinion/observation networks.
  • Patterns: Letta recall/core/archival, A-Mem evolving, Graphiti incremental. Platforms: Cognee (ECL), mem0 (~10% retention), Zep (bitemporal, P95 ≈300 ms).
  • MEM1: memory learned via RL — budgets as signal, reward task success; 7B beats 70B.
  • DevOps memory: episode/temporal/knowledge vocabularies, 24-h windows, 4-h lookback, Nova Forge BYOO, four emergent behaviors.

Chapter 5

Reasoning and Planning

≈ 6 mintwo axes · PathRAG / R3-RAG · Outlines · event-driven orchestration · RPG

The chapter opens on the industry’s loudest argument — Anthropic’s multi-agent research system versus Cognition’s “Don’t Build Multi-Agents” — and dismisses it. Production agents fail not from the wrong agent count but from inability to (1) decide what to do next, (2) represent state and constraints, (3) verify steps, (4) recover when reality disagrees. The tell is LangGraph itself: control flow is the real product. Cemri et al. (2025, “Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?”) analyze 1,600+ annotated traces, find 14 unique failure modes, and show multi-step reliability dropping into single digits when the workflow is underspecified. Hence the thesis: “Agentic AI looks like artificial intelligence, but it behaves like process engineering.” The LLM is a probabilistic execution engine inside the loop; a prompt is a poor substitute for flowchart + state machine + guardrails.

Two axes, not one autonomy dial

Multistep workflows have three constraints — State, Structure, Scale — and the design space has two independently tuned axes: context control and workflow autonomy. Horizontal workflow graphs manage execution flow — “your process flow diagram, made executable”; vertical knowledge graphs organize domain knowledge — “your data model and business rules engine.” The agentic balance: workflow graphs = how to think, knowledge graphs = what to know, structured outputs = how to communicate. Lorenz’s imaginary space frames it: in structured representation, thinking looks like movement — traversal a mental action, path exploration a simulated decision, a transition a commitment. In the wild, every production coding agent implements the dual graph — Claude Code’s CLAUDE.md vertical, its bash loop horizontal; Cherny credits shell self-verification with a 200%–300% quality improvement.

Graph structure doesn’t guarantee semantic validity. Three cascading failures: semantic drift (“The restaurant manages the chef” — valid syntax, nonsense, compounding exponentially), hallucination propagation, domain violations. OntoMetric (Yu et al., 2026, ESG KGs) quantifies the fix: error falls from 83.3% unconstrained to 19.44% with ontological validation — domain/range checks, inference rules, consistency checking.

The retrieval defense stack

The enemy first: the distracting effect (Amiraz et al., 2025) — similar-but-irrelevant passages flip abstention to confident error, and reranking amplifies it (retrievers return semantically related, answerless passages). Dangers: error amplification, action irreversibility, context pollution, self-correction failure. The defenses:

  • PathRAG (Chen et al., 2025) retrieves relational paths, not passages: structural verification (paths must exist in the KG), flow-based pruning (resources decay with graph distance), reliability scoring (defaults alpha=0.8, threshold=0.05, top_k=15). On a verified path — Jane Smith → enrolled_in → Policy #POL-456789 → … → “prudent layperson standard met” — “the agent cannot accidentally jump to the Gold Plan’s provisions because there is no edge.”
  • R3-RAG (Li, 2025) learns via RL when/what to retrieve and how to decompose, with dual rewards (outcome ±1.0; process = relevance × format). 52.6% average multi-hop QA accuracy, +15% over baselines; the learned policy picks retrieve_paths / decompose_then_retrieve / skip_retrieval — a cognitive immune system: routine copay = one lookup; appendectomy = multi-hop; “Is this ER visit covered?” = three parallel retrievals (St. Mary’s network status, Silver emergency authorization, inpatient benefit limits).
  • Microsoft’s three-tier taxonomy: Foundation — Basic Retriever, Parent-Child Retriever, Hypothetical Question Retriever; Integration — Cypher Templates, Dynamic Cypher Generation, Text2Cypher; Advanced — Graph-Enhanced Vector Search, Global Community Summary Retriever.

The chapter’s capstone domain is insurance claims — Jane Smith’s emergency appendectomy at out-of-network St. Mary’s Hospital, the Gold Plan’s 90% rate planted as the distractor, and a mid-case coordination-of-benefits pivot (employer change six weeks prior; coverage overlap March 1–15). Conflicting signals → HITL refinement with a claims examiner.

Nodes must pivot mid-execution — interleaved thinking. MiniMax-M2: preserving prior-round thinking state lifts SWE-bench Verified 69.4 vs 67.2, Tau² 87 vs 64 (+35.9%), BrowseComp 44.0 vs 31.4 (+40.1%). Helps analysis, diagnostic, research, and planning nodes; adds little for transaction-processing or compliance nodes, where auditable predictability is the point.

Structured generation: the keystone

Most graph-system agent failures come from internode communication breakdowns, not bad reasoning. Outlines builds an FSM over valid token sequences and zeroes invalid tokens — true zero-shot structured generation, no retry loops, guaranteed nested structures; compound effects: unbreakable internode contracts, exact structural-consistency metrics, composable reasoning. Per node type: reasoning (premises/inference steps/confidence), planning (preconditions/parameters/outcomes/rollback), action (valid API calls), validation (violations/severity/remediation). Claims decision fields — determination, approved amount, patient responsibility, EOB code, regulatory basis, appeal rights — can’t be emitted incomplete: 0.1% malformed is compliance exposure; grammar-constrained decoding makes it zero. Valid by construction.

🧭 Book framework

Pipeline patterns: sequential (strict dependencies), loop (validity-checked retries, recursion_limit=10), tree (Send-API fan-out) — plus hybrids: dynamic selection, nested composition, graceful degradation (“a feature, not an error case”).

Event-driven orchestration

The fourth architecture. In-process shared memory holds under ~50 tasks/day; beyond that, synchronous agent-to-agent calls recreate early-2010s microservices mistakes — the “distributed monolith” (Pourshahid, Solace). Fix: agents become stateless subscribers to an event backbone (Kafka, Redis Streams, SQS); no agent knows another exists. Four layers: Layer 0 State (external stores: database, KG); Layer 1 Event backbone (durable, ordered, replayable); Layer 2 Agents (stateless, one capability each); Layer 3 Meta-orchestrator (reads all topics; detects stuck agents via consumer lag, poison pills via the same message retried five times, 80% throughput drops). Three capabilities: fault isolation, replay-and-recovery (reset the offset, replay through fixed code), framework interoperability. CQRS: writes through the backbone, reads straight to the KG. Trade-off: not worth it for a solo dev at ~20 events/day.

Planning — and its empirical validation

Separate planning from execution: the planning node gets tool descriptions but no bindings — pure strategy; the plan is an explicit, auditable artifact. Escalating patterns: hierarchical planning via hypertree decomposition (60 sequential steps → 4×15 parallel tracks); constraint-guided planning (ConstraintExtractor → PlanValidator → refine below threshold); dynamic DAG construction from task dependencies with explicit parallelism factors. Microsoft’s Repository Planning Graph validates this at scale: ZeroRepo averages 36,000 LOC (3.9× Claude Code, 64× baselines) at 81.5% functional coverage and 69.7% test pass rate (+27.3/+35.8), scaling near-linearly past 1,100 leaf features while natural-language plans “rapidly accumulate inconsistencies.” RPG-Encoder (repository → graph) hits 93.7% function-level localization on SWE-bench Verified (+14.4) and cuts incremental maintenance overhead 95.7%. On multi-agent: “Parallelism itself isn’t the enemy — uncoordinated parallelism is.” Controlled parallelism = sequential planning → independence verification → a parallel window (PathRAG-validated queries, structured outputs, response-masked behaviors) → ontologically validated merge → sequential decision. Anthropic’s 90.2% improvement is orchestrated, not free.

DevOps capstone: the diagnostician

The capstone adds only a reasoning layer atop Chapter 3’s KG and Chapter 4’s memory — six SRE phases: alert triage → evidence collection → hypothesis formation → hypothesis testing → root cause confirmation → remediation planning. Design choice: workflow state never duplicates infrastructure knowledge; nodes query KG and memory at decision time. The walkthrough: checkout latency 200 ms → 2.5 s. Triage: payment errors, DB timeouts, three services, two SLAs >99.9%, one drift item → high severity. Evidence: a DB config deployment 2 hours prior, a payment restart 4 hours prior. Hypotheses ranked by structural plausibility × historical frequency, filtered by the capability model. Parallel tests: pool at 100% utilization, 47 waiting threads; memory normal → confirm connection-pool exhaustion, skip network partition. Confirmation: the deployment cut max connections 100 → 20; a bitemporal CAUSED_BY edge records itself; remediation runs three tiers of homoiconic OperationalRules. Total: three minutes — and the consolidated pattern strengthens for next time. The closing model, “graph planned and event executed”: the workflow graph computes order (topological sort, critical path, parallelization windows), the execution layer runs it, results reshape the graph — plan, execute, feedback, repeat. Monolithic prompt chains’ “8% task completion rates aren’t competitive.”

Project status GraphOps can reason: the six-phase DAG diagnoses the connection-pool exhaustion in the fixture in three simulated minutes. Next: give it hands (Ch. 6).

Takeaways

  • Multi-agent vs single-agent is a false choice; reliability = graph coordination + reasoning/planning — “graph planned and event executed.”
  • Two axes: context control × workflow autonomy; how to think / what to know / how to communicate.
  • Retrieval defense: distracting effect (reranking amplifies) → PathRAG → R3-RAG → Microsoft’s three-tier taxonomy.
  • Outlines is the keystone: malformed output mathematically impossible — valid by construction.
  • Event-driven: four layers, the “distributed monolith” anti-pattern, fault isolation / replay / interoperability; CQRS.
  • RPG/ZeroRepo validate graph planning: 36k LOC, 81.5% coverage, 93.7% localization; uncoordinated parallelism is the enemy.

Chapter 6

Agentic Graph-Based Tool Orchestration

≈ 6 minprompt bloat · RAG-MCP → gateway → COLT · three primitives · tools as graph nodes · IFC

“Intelligence without the ability to act is merely contemplation.” LLMs do one operation — text to text; minds without hands. The breakthrough: treat tools as interconnected data in a knowledge graph, not hardcoded logic, with the Model Context Protocol as the practical foundation — discovery and invocation via two operations, tools/list and tools/call, so “systems become fluid rather than rigid.” The spec mandates OAuth 2.x with the authorization server (token issuance) separated from the resource server (validating tokens). And since tools/call doesn’t care what sits behind a name, whole agents masquerade as tools — AWS Spring AI’s AirlineAgentTool orchestrates internally, appears as one capability.

The prompt bloat crisis

MCP’s success makes organizations expose everything, and every description eats the context window. RAG-MCP’s stress tests (Gan and Sun, 2025): 10 tools, near-perfect selection; 100, noticeable degradation; 1,000, accuracy below 40%. Block’s Goose in production — 12,000+ employees, 60+ MCP servers — watched employees enable everything “just in case”; Microsoft’s Core AI team treats bloat as inevitable, requiring RAG-based tool selection. Hence a ladder:

  • RAG-MCP: Retrieval (a lightweight retriever searches a tool-metadata index), Validation (synthetic queries), Invocation (only selected descriptions injected). Prompt tokens drop 50%–70% (2,134 → 1,084); selection accuracy rises 13.62% → 43.13%.
  • Gateway pattern (Dallezotte et al., 2025): a reverse-proxy control plane turns many-to-many into hub-and-spoke. WRITER’s enterprise gateway ingests OpenAPI specs and Postman collections, refines descriptions with Palmyra X5, distills the tool surface into two metatools — search and execute — descriptions never enter the prompt.
  • Toolshed (Lumer et al., 2024): enhanced representations — name, description, argument schema, synthetic queries, key topics — 95%+ selection accuracy at 3,500+ tools, no fine-tuning.
  • COLT (Baidu, Qu et al., 2024): tasks need tool sets, modeled as three interconnected graphs — query-scene, scene-tool, query-tool. “Gold price + 1M AMZN stocks valued in CNY” returns all three tools as one solution set. Completeness ~48% → 70%; recall 59% → 85%.

Governance context (Fersht, HFS/Cognizant 2025): 73% of agentic-AI organizations run multi-agent systems, averaging 12 agents; governance consistently fails above 5.

Skills: the judgment layer

A skill is a reusable procedure encoding when and how to use tools — ordering, pre/post checks, failure modes — versus a bare capability. Anthropic’s Agent Skills specification (2025): SKILL.md + YAML frontmatter, progressive disclosure (metadata only, ~100 tokens; full contents on selection), no installation, nontechnical authors. Quality data: SkillsBench (DAIR.AI) — curated skills +16.2% task performance; self-generated unreviewed, zero; 2–3 per task optimal. SkillNet (Liang et al., 2026) rates 200,000+ skills on five dimensions — Safety, Completeness, Executability, Maintainability, Cost awareness — for 40% higher rewards, 30% fewer steps, model-agnostic. Counterpoint SkillRL: small evolved skill banks compress tokens 10–20× (7B + hierarchical SkillBank = 89.9% ALFWorld). Practical: quality-gated retrieval — safety and executability weighted 2×, Neo4j vector top-20, min_quality 0.6, ranked by relevance × quality; the threshold is a risk knob (research ~0.4, healthcare 0.8+).

Three primitives, one gradient

🧭 Book framework

Ngiam’s taxonomy — the book’s Table 6-2: Skills encode judgment (what to do, in what order; ~100 tokens; everyone; no auth model). CLIs encode composable execution (how to perform the operation; ~400 tokens after dynamic discovery; developers in build mode; native piping; on-device tokens). MCPs encode authenticated access (how to connect securely; 23,000–50,000 tokens of schema without RAG; enterprise/background agents; OAuth 2.x built-in).

CLIs are the oldest pattern (Unix pipes, 1973), already internalized by models (Dharmesh Shah, 2026); MCP arrived November 2024. CLI-Anything (HKU-DS): every piece of software has a latent agent interface with four LLM-friendly properties — structured input, structured output, self-description (--help = discovery without a registry), determinism. The deployment gradient is Ngiam’s own setups: personal — 12 skills, a handful of CLIs, 4 MCP servers; work — 16 skills, almost no CLIs, 10+ MCP servers with OS-level sandboxes and per-agent allowed_tools scoping. More stakeholders and unsupervised agents shift you CLI-heavy → MCP-heavy; skills stay constant; per-agent access control is least privilege, complementary to IFC: “IFC governs data flow; access control governs tool availability.” Convergence: Google Workspace CLI (2026) — CLI + MCP server mode + 100+ skills. Tip: profile each workflow on who/when/where/access; skills first.

Tools as graph nodes — dependencies, types, and information flow

RAG finds a tool but not its dependencies, I/O types, or data flow. Neo4j’s “Going Meta” moves definitions into the graph: a Tool node storing metadata and its nested Cypher implementation, linked HAS_TOOL from a Class node — domain experts add tools without code. Type matching becomes traversal: the NESTFUL benchmark (Basu et al., 2025) shows the best LLMs reach only ~41% on nested API calls — they miss that COVID statistics need a country code first. The graph fix: REQUIRES_INPUT (parameter location, type ISO_3166_1_alpha_2) and PRODUCES_OUTPUT (field short_name, same type) meet at a shared DataType node, and a MATCH path discovers the chain — India → “IN” → covid stats: “from probabilistic guessing to deterministic pathfinding.”

Security beyond authentication is FIDES (Costa et al., 2025): Information Flow Control over chained tools — taint tracking (TRUSTED/UNTRUSTED labels propagate; mixing inherits UNTRUSTED; policy blocks sensitive actions) and opaque variable management (the LLM sees a UUID reference, must call read_variable). IFC counters what OAuth cannot: agent tool misuse and goal manipulation. Self-evolution closes the loop: usage analytics (ToolUsage nodes) feed pattern recognition (co-occurrence — pairs sharing >10 sessions), then automated improvement (suggest_composite_tool, gated by validate_cypher, derived_from lineage). Trust must be earned — keyword stuffing means “surfacing the best marketers rather than the best tools” — so verification-based trust (enumerable, typed capabilities) plus performance-based scores. Baidu’s DRAFT closes doc-vs-reality gaps in three phases (experience gathering, learning from experience, documentation rewriting) — the system discovers truth anyway. Metatooling — tools creating tools — shows three emergent levels: composition, modification (80% response-time gains), full generation.

Orchestration at scale, and the missing governance layer

Four patterns: the intelligent orchestrator exposes one tool hiding everything (intent → five years of patterns → compliance-verified rules → a 30-minute human task, confidence 0.94); hierarchical orchestration routes through domain orchestrators, escalating cross-domain when confidence < 0.8; functional clustering (Baidu) embeds tools by what they do, K-means++ into toolkits so failover swaps in a functionally equivalent tool; the Enterprise AI OS layers PermissionManager → InformationFlowController → ContextIntegrator → SemanticSearch → ActionGovernor (human approval tiers) → execute_with_audit. The missing layer is context governance: Baselga documented one developer’s coherent context architecture becoming five divergent ones at team scale (“the unexpected tax,” Ben Erez); agents amplify divergence “at the speed of token generation.” The federated fix has three layers: configuration as code (Daniel Meppiel’s APM; syntactic consistency), a shared knowledge layer (Arlan Rakhmetzhanov’s Nia Skills; factual consistency), a governance control plane (Daniel Jarjoura’s Runtime; behavioral consistency): “Context failure, not AI failure.”

DevOps finale: hands

Chapter 2’s opaque get_metrics node becomes real tooling. QueryMetricsAPI registers as a graph node (endpoint, oauth2_service_account, rate limit, timeout), linked HAS_TOOL from every metrics-enabled Service, with REQUIRES_INPUT typed to Service.canonical_id — sourced from the graph itself; adding a tool or service means adding nodes, not code. Pydantic MetricsQuery/MetricsResult (fixed Literal metric set; bounded step_seconds) reject malformed output like “response time” pre-call. Then orchestrated_investigation replays Chapter 5’s checkout incident with live tools: discovery via HAS_TOOL; a structured latency_p99 query spanning alert −2 h to +30 min; parallel DEPENDS_ON saturation queries via asyncio.gather — saturation > 0.9 flags the payments-db, and with Chapter 5’s 100→20 knowledge, “the root cause is confirmed by data.” Bridge to Chapter 7: was the action correct?

Project status GraphOps has hands: tools are graph data, calls are schema-validated, and the saturation check confirms the payments-db connection pool in the fixture. Next: judge itself (Ch. 7).

Takeaways

  • Tools are data in the graph — contextual discovery, dependency matching, IFC security, self-evolution.
  • Prompt bloat (10/100/1,000 tools → <40%; Block Goose); ladder: RAG-MCP → gateway metatools → Toolshed → COLT.
  • Three primitives: skills = judgment (~100 tokens), CLIs = execution (~400), MCPs = authenticated access (23k–50k).
  • Defense in depth: OAuth caller, FIDES IFC, DRAFT verification, per-agent allowed_tools.
  • Context governance, federated: APM / Nia Skills / Runtime — “Context failure, not AI failure.”
  • GraphOps acts on real tools; Ch. 7 asks: was the action correct?

Chapter 7

Self-Evolution and Evaluation

≈ 6 minexecution graph · 4-layer cognitive autopsy · semantic backpropagation · RPO + GVP · stripe-python autopsy

The agent built so far can think but not learn: it fails surprisingly, degrades silently. The fix leverages graph complexity three ways — reasoning becomes a queryable artifact (the execution graph), failure gets a coordinate system (node, edge, pathway), and dependency mapping enables coherent safe evolution — the basis of semantic backpropagation.

The execution graph is the dynamic counterpart of Chapter 5’s workflow graph — “blueprint versus autobiography”: an immutable per-query record whose nodes carry type (LLM_Call, Tool_Invocation, Retrieval, Decision_Point), timestamps, payloads, latency/token/cost metrics, causal parent-child edges. Not logging — queryable. Implementation: OpenTelemetry spans in Neo4j via a two-phase write — the node and its :TRIGGERED edge created before execution so causal structure survives failure, metrics after.

The four-layer cognitive autopsy

One warning: criteria drift (Shankar et al., 2024, “Who Validates the Validators?”) — criteria and outputs co-define each other; derive categories from 50–100 reviewed traces (open, then axial coding). The layers:

  1. Layer 0 — zero-shot hallucination gate. GLiClass (Knowledgator, 2025): zero-shot NLI — graph-materialized context as premise, answer as hypothesis, no fine-tuning. Three hallucination sources: insufficient knowledge (parametric memory fills KG gaps), inadequate context (too few hops), excessive context (50 nodes for a 5-node question). Threshold 0.85 → BLOCK_AND_REGENERATE; catches 60–70% of hallucinations at <5% of judge compute. The SLM-LLM flywheel: uncertain scores (0.5–0.85) escalate upward and become the small model’s training data.
  2. Layer 1 — context sufficiency. Failure here is retrieval/KG, not reasoning: did the agent possess what it needed? Sufficient context (Joren et al., 2025): Completeness, Contradiction, Ambiguity. Judge per Meta’s J1 approach (Whitehouse et al., 2025), rewarded for a reasoning trace before a JSON verdict; validate against expert labels to >90% agreement; verdicts binary, never numeric.
  3. Layer 2 — cognitive fault isolation. Knowledge failures (coherent reasoning over wrong facts) vs reasoning failures (right facts, broken logic). Knowledge: MICRO-ACT’s DECOMPOSE (Huo et al., 2025) splits conflicts into atomic claims scored by a Knowledge Index. Reasoning: InfoGain(i) = P(Answer | reasoning_up_to_step_i) − P(Answer | reasoning_up_to_step_i−1) — near-zero marks redundancy, non sequiturs, circularity.
  4. Layer 3 — tool-integrated reasoning judge. TIR-Judge (Xu et al., 2026) interleaves reasoning with Python execution and generates Cypher against the KG — agents “carry their own ground truth in a queryable structure.” Reward = correctness × format × tool_accuracy, deliberately multiplicative: a well-formatted wrong answer scores zero. TIR-Judge-8B matches reward models 4× its size.

Output: a JSON diagnostic report — verdict, per-layer findings, recommended intervention, target nodes — “what drives the self-improvement engine.” Truthfulness: dual-pathway analysis (Luo et al., 2026) — Q-anchored pathways route question→answer; A-anchored pathways judge the answer’s own plausibility, where hallucinations originate. Mixture-of-probes reaches >75% AUC; pathway reweighting adds +10%. The actionable field pathway_classification: Q-anchored failure → fine-tuning; A-anchored failure → better retrieval — retrieval alone can’t kill A-anchored hallucination.

Beyond the layers: user-behavior signals (Han et al., 2025, RLUF: reformulation, copy/paste, session success, frustration); InfoGain shape (“Aha!” spike = brittle, “grinding” = brute force, S-curve = reliable); circuit discovery (Conmy et al., 2023) stays out of production — >80% only on narrow failure types, so stop at Layer 2; model size (Cheng et al., 2024): small models trust retrieved context, 70B-class favor parametric priors.

From diagnosis to intervention

The self-evolution taxonomy (Gao et al., 2026) crosses four axes: what — model, context (rewire edges, merge nodes, prune subgraphs: the graph is “not just the target but the medium”), tool, architecture (“graph surgery”) — × when (intra-test-time, sub-second vs inter-test-time) × how (reward-based, imitation-based, population-based) — × where (general-purpose vs domain-specialized). The intervention trilogy: prompt refinement for localized low-InfoGain failures; fine-tuning for systemic knowledge gaps (consistently low KI); structural constraint for FORMAT_VIOLATION/ParseError — attach an Outlines schema so the error becomes impossible. Routing: insufficient context → RETRIEVAL_FIX; format violation → STRUCTURAL_CONSTRAINT; reasoning failure with ≤2 low-InfoGain steps and KI >0.8 → PROMPT_REFINEMENT; else FINE_TUNE — deterministic and auditable.

Semantic backpropagation descends from TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024 — textual feedback as gradient): a structured description of the required change flows backward through the execution graph. The book’s contribution is neighbor-awareness — feedback for node v includes all other predecessors’ outputs of its successor w, preventing the misassignment above. The division of labor:

  • SEAL (Zweiger et al., 2025) turns failures into curricula — each: same-domain, the trap, a correct trace, the labeled critical step.
  • AgentEvolver (Tongyi Lab, 2025) shifts passive→active learning — self-questioning (traverse sparse KG regions; largest gain, +20.3%), self-navigating (similarity by reasoning structure), self-attributing (credit via execution-graph causality, α≈0.6) — Qwen2.5-7B: 15.8% → 45.2% on WebArena, zero human-annotated data.
  • SICA (Robeyns et al., 2025) does code-level self-modification, SWE-bench Verified 17% → 53%, guarded by a 50/25/25 utility and an async overseer with veto.
  • TPT (think-prune-train) mines successes — sample at temperatures 0.3–0.9, prune to traces correct and KI >0.85 and avg InfoGain >0.15, keep the top 10–20%.
  • Reflect-Retry-Reward (Bensal et al., 2025) is real-time metacognitive debugging — reward the reflection by alignment with ground truth (0.3/0.4/0.3); tracks first-attempt recovery rate.
  • XSkill (Jiang et al., 2026): dual-stream augmentation — action-level Experiences and task-level Skills cut tool errors 29.9% → 16.3%, lift success 33.6% → 40.3% (90-day decay).
  • Cognee makes skills self-improving graph objects (add → cognify → search → learn; .amendify() writes evidence-grounded amendments); routing ranks by demonstrated success — 3 clean canary successes outrank 50 executions at 40% failure.

The evolutionary loop, made safe

The flywheel: execute → evaluate → backpropagate + select intervention → candidate (prompt-library update, fine-tune, or output schema) → graduated validation → deploy or archive. Under RPO: Recursion (improvement mechanisms themselves improvable), Provenance (changes signed to an immutable ledger — “source control for thought,” instant rollback), Optimization = the graduated validation protocol, three tiers: Tier 1 canary (~1% traffic; prompt/hyperparameter changes; target-metric gain, no core-KPI degradation, auto-rollback), Tier 2 staging gauntlet (SEAL/TPT fine-tunes and tool integrations pass benchmark + regression + safety/alignment + performance suites under U = w1·accuracy + w2·(1−cost) + w3·safety), Tier 3 airlock (safety-protocol changes, new tools, high-potential failures: sandboxed, human approval).

Kepler (OpenAI, 2026) splits a dual store — curated, human-authored Knowledge vs ephemeral agent-generated Learnings — with a daily garbage-collection agent (resolved, contradicted, or unretrieved in 30 days; evidence: 3 engineers, ~1M lines/5 months). LEANAGENT (Kumarappan et al., 2025) supplies the circuit breakers — WF-5 halt >3%, CFR <0.90, backward transfer (graph shortcuts), plasticity (declining IP = calcification). The meta-skill is loop engineering — Cherny: “I don’t prompt Claude anymore. I have loops running that prompt Claude.” The graph makes loops strong: execution graph as failure coordinates, KG as judge ground truth, workflow graph as feedback topology, provenance ledger as itself a graph.

⚠ Pitfall

Known failure modes: reward-hacked SEAL data (validate against held-out real failures), catastrophic forgetting from synthetic regression suites, evaluation overhead, and validation misfires — “a 20% canary is a partial rollout, not a canary.”

DevOps capstone: the premature-closure autopsy

A routine stripe-python 3.2.1 → 3.3.0 deploys to checkout-service. Context: it calls payments.charge()/retrieve(), upstream of order- and fulfillment-service; the changelog deprecates synchronous batch_charge, adds async payment methods, changes the default connection timeout 30 → 10 s. The agent predicts: “API contract violation,” HIGH, confidence 0.78. The SRE finds no batch_charge usage, approves — and twenty minutes later connection timeouts cascade. The prediction was partially correct: right pathway and severity, wrong mechanism — connection-pool exhaustion from the timeout reduction under load. The autopsy: Layer 1: context sufficient (0.97); KI 0.91. The InfoGain trace convicts reasoning — identify_api_changes 0.34, map_to_service_methods 0.29, assess_deprecation_impact 0.22, select_primary_failure_mode 0.03, assign_confidence −0.01, generate_recommendation 0.19: premature closure at CausalAttributionNode — a reasoning failure, not a knowledge gap → PROMPT_REFINEMENT. Neighbor-aware feedback carries ChangelogRetrieval’s output (all three changes, including the timeout) and KnowledgeGraphQuery’s output (no batch_charge usage), rewriting the prompt to score API versus configuration changes as co-equal hypotheses. It passes the Tier 1 canary; the next week a pool-size reduction is flagged co-equal — no incident.

Project status GraphOps learns: the autopsy isolates premature closure, backprop rewrites the prompt neighbor-aware, canary promotes. Next: make it affordable and governable (Ch. 8).

Takeaways

  • The execution graph — immutable, queryable, two-phase-written — gives every query failure coordinates.
  • Autopsy: GLiClass gate (0.85) → J1 sufficient-context judge (binary) → KI + InfoGain → TIR-Judge (multiplicative reward).
  • Semantic backpropagation must be neighbor-aware (TextGrad lineage) or credit assignment is wrong.
  • Deterministic interventions — prompt / fine-tune / structural constraint; SEAL failures, TPT successes, RRR live recovery, XSkill/Cognee knowledge.
  • The loop is safe under RPO + GVP (canary / gauntlet / airlock); Kepler GC + LEANAGENT metrics as entropy controls.
  • stripe-python autopsy: premature closure at InfoGain 0.03 → neighbor-aware fix → canary → next-week catch.

Chapter 8

Optimization

≈ 6 minselective intelligence · subgraph RBAC · schema evolution · GPU & KV cache · the completed agent

The agent works in a notebook — “then someone asks what it costs to run.” Production is where three forces collide: cost, governance, performance — taking the DevOps agent from prototype to intelligent, self-improving, cost-effective, secure, real-time.

Selective intelligence

The economic principle: a federation of specialists — small cheap models for routine work, large models only where needed. Quality holds or improves — “you just stop overpaying for it.” A 3B SLM is 10–30× cheaper per token than its 405B sibling (Belcak et al., 2025). The map: classification → a fine-tuned 3B; extraction → Triplex, a 3.8B model outperforming GPT-4o at KG construction at one-sixtieth the cost; retrieval routing and validation → small models or logic rules; only open-ended synthesis, complex causal reasoning, and novel problems need frontier — typically 10–20% of invocations. NVIDIA’s paper adds the SLM edge: predictability (front-door router). Routing matures in three stages: static by node type (“most teams should start here”); threshold cascading à la FrugalGPT (smallest first, escalate below a confidence threshold; a synthesis node might serve ~50% cheapest / 30% midtier / 20% frontier; calibration is the challenge); learned routing — RouteLLM: >2× cost reduction retaining 95% of GPT-4 quality; MixLLM: 97% of GPT-4 quality at 24% of the cost. Static plus cascading covers 80% of the benefit with 20% of the complexity.

Two metrics: cost per successful completion (not per token — a cheap model failing 40% isn’t cheaper) and a quality-parity threshold per node (validation demands >99% — wrong validation is worse than none; a query analyst tolerates 90%). Eval sets are per node, from production data — MMLU doesn’t predict your alert taxonomy — with asymmetric failure weights (missed P1, P1→P3 = 10.0; false escalation, P3→P1 = 1.0). Kakao’s AI Shopping Mate: GPT-4o everywhere scored 0.655 format / 0.578 accuracy; fine-tuned 27–32B models per node hit 0.987 / 0.890 — and across 2,100 human-evaluated turns, the smaller fine-tuned models were preferred in 63% of cases.

Governance

“In a graph, everything is reachable from everything else. That is the point. It is also the governance problem” — one unscoped query can traverse public catalog → cost data → employee records. Three defenses. Subgraph access control: Neo4j Enterprise privileges at label, relationship-type, and property level (DENY READ {cost_per_hour, budget_code}; DENY TRAVERSE Employee, Compensation), with security transparency: a forbidden node is invisible, not access-denied — probing boundaries leaks nothing. PII and retention: GDPR/CCPA deletion cascades through dense graphs, so Rehmer’s “Privacy by Architecture” keeps only UUIDs + relationships in the KG, PII in an Identity Store; Article 17 erasure = a single-row update — soft delete (mask the mapping; an anonymous orphan remains) or hard delete (DETACH DELETE). Execution graph as compliance artifact: KG.GOV (Meroño-Peñuela et al., 2025) encodes governance metadata in the reasoning graph — sources accessed, access role, pii_accessed, model ID/version, decision confidence, human-review flags, retention policy. One role per agent persona; Mohamed et al. (2024): approaches are engine-coupled — plan a policy abstraction layer.

Production maintenance

Four mechanics:

  • Schema evolution — graph databases lack ALTER TABLE; schema-optional graphs drift silently. Neo4j-Migrations (Simons) is the Flyway equivalent, migration history stored as a subgraph in the database itself (V003__add_monitored_by_relationship.cypher: promote alert_config into AlertRule nodes + MONITORED_BY edges). Zero-downtime: init-container migrations and N−1 compatibility — add alongside, remove later.
  • Node/edge lifecycle — CrowdStrike’s Threat Graph is append-only with TTL (40+ petabytes, 70M requests/second — never update, expire in the background; new node versions, not in-place edits), while Graphiti uses temporal invalidation: conflicts set t_invalid, never delete — invalidate the stripe-python 3.2.1 DEPENDS_ON edge, MERGE the 3.3.0 edge, and “what did infrastructure look like before the change” stays answerable. Pruning needs care — 200 resources at 5-minute intervals = 57,600 nodes/day; tier retention (7 days full → hourly → daily; permanent hubs).
  • Incremental updates — LightRAG (Guo et al., 2025) runs new documents through the same extraction pipeline, enriching existing entities — update cost proportional to new data, not graph size (its edge over GraphRAG’s community reconstruction).
  • Staged rollout — three independently versioned components (schema, data, agent code), four phases: migrations with N−1, backfill, code behind a canary (5% / 2 h; promote when the regression suite passes, p95 < 500 ms, accuracy delta ≥ −0.02), cleanup after 7 days. depends_on ordering ties this to the GVP.

Hardware: honest scope

Two channels bottleneck: traversals and inference — memory bandwidth, a natural GPU fit: cuGraph PageRank up to 137× CPU, Louvain 125× over NetworkX; nx-cugraph is a drop-in backend — LiveJournal betweenness 7 minutes → 5 seconds (485×). The caveat: no major graph DB executes Cypher/Gremlin traversal on GPU — the pattern is extract subgraph → GPU analytics → write back as properties (PageRank → criticality_score → “top 20% of services”). Inference: parallelizing across the DAG is cheapest; vLLM’s continuous batching plus multi-LoRA serves many fine-tuned specialists from one base on one GPU (50–80 ms TTFT at 100 concurrent users); Cerebras runs Llama 3.1 8B at 1,800 tokens/second (20× GPU cloud, verified to 75×); SambaNova’s SN50 hot-swaps specialists in milliseconds. The constraint is the KV cache: peak KV per active user — not model size — sets concurrency per H100; quantizing weights doesn’t help. Microsoft’s Memento (2026; SFT on 228,000 traces) teaches block-summarized chain-of-thought — a sawtooth KV pattern cutting peak KV 2–2.5×, blocks 5–20×: ten GPUs become four. Latency budgets: traversal 5–50 ms, SLM step 50–200 ms, a 5–10-call workflow 0.5–2 s parallelized, single-digit seconds for 30+ calls.

The completed agent

Table 8-1’s arc — twin (Ch. 3) → memory (4) → investigation DAGs (5) → MCP tooling (6) → learning (7) → production readiness (8). The per-node config: AlertClassifier and LogParser on 3B LoRA specialists (1/30th each); DependencyAnalyzer on 8B (1/10th); CausalAttributionNode — the node that failed in Chapter 7 — on a cascade, 8B escalating to Claude Sonnet below 0.7 confidence (~30% of the time; ~1/5th blended); PredictionSynthesis on frontier (1×, justified). Only synthesis consistently uses frontier; blended cost per prediction drops ~80%. GPU blast-radius analysis takes DEPENDS_ON|CALLS*1..4 from 3–5 s to under 100 ms; roles are enforced (sre_oncall reads no cost fields; finance_analyst the mirror image), and the execution graph records the role per query — the audit trail. handle_deployment_event runs six steps, each annotated with its pillars: classify → parse → incremental KG update + GPU blast radius → cascaded causal attribution → frontier synthesis → governance-annotated execution graph; steps 1–3 parallel. End to end: under 2 seconds, ~$0.002 per event versus $0.01+ frontier-everywhere. Pitfalls: edge cases routed beyond a model’s competence, overpruned KGs, governance blocking reasoning, uncoordinated schema migrations, wrong evaluation sets, GPU cold-start.

The book’s conclusion

Chapter 1 named five vector-RAG flaws; Chapter 2 answered with strings-to-things, the dual-graph architecture, and eight pillars; Part II built the brain (representation, memory); Part III enabled action (reasoning, planning, tools, structured output); Part IV made it viable (learning loop, then cost/governance/performance). The stripe-python upgrade that would have woken an SRE at 3:00 a.m. is handled autonomously. The adoption test is four questions: meaningful relationships? multistep reasoning? must the system improve over time? are cost/governance/latency real constraints? Adoption is modular — knowledge graph first, temporal memory next, the workflow graph when single prompts hit their ceiling. Outlook: model swaps become configuration changes; graph DBs gain native AI features; ContextGraphs (Vanderseypen, 2026) push schema-as-code to the device — .pg schemas in Git, structured-interface traversal instead of Cypher, ACID, time travel; MCP is maturing; evaluation is becoming a discipline. From teams like AnyShift and Kakao: “You have the blueprint and the build. The rest is engineering.”

Project status GraphOps complete: the 3 a.m. incident diagnoses autonomously in under 2 seconds at ~$0.002 — the 45-minute SRE run is retired.

Takeaways

  • Selective intelligence: federation of specialists; static → FrugalGPT cascade → RouteLLM/MixLLM; cost-per-successful-completion + quality-parity thresholds; Kakao.
  • Governance triad: subgraph RBAC (forbidden = invisible), Privacy-by-Architecture UUID/Identity-Store, execution graph as compliance artifact (KG.GOV).
  • Maintenance: Neo4j-Migrations with N−1; CrowdStrike TTL vs Graphiti invalidation; LightRAG incremental; four-phase rollout.
  • Hardware honesty: GPUs accelerate analytics (extract → analyze → write-back), not Cypher; the KV cache binds concurrency (Memento).
  • Completed agent: 3B LoRA → 8B → cascade → frontier; ~80% cost cut; <2 s, ~$0.002 per event.
  • Adoption test — four questions; start modular. “You have the blueprint and the build. The rest is engineering.”

Adopt? The book’s four questions

  1. Do your data contain meaningful relationships that queries must respect?
  2. Do you need multistep reasoning over those relationships?
  3. Must the system improve over time from its own experience?
  4. Are cost, governance, and latency real constraints?

Adoption is modular — knowledge graph first (Ch. 3), temporal memory next (Ch. 4), the workflow graph when single prompts hit their ceiling (Ch. 5). Further reading, per the book itself: supplemental material — code examples, exercises, and more — at github.com/AnthonyAlcaraz/agentic-graph-rag-skills.

💡 If you read only 5 pages

A five-stop tour:

  • Ch. 2, Table 2-1 + Figure 2-1 — the five flaws → eight pillars, and the dual-graph loop: the thesis in two artifacts.
  • Ch. 3, Figure 3-2 + the OWA/CWA passage — the three-graph architecture, and why SHACL pre-action shapes are agent safety.
  • Ch. 4, the four memory operations (Figure 4-3) — consolidation, indexing, supersede-don’t-delete, RRF-fused retrieval.
  • Ch. 5, PathRAG + “graph planned and event executed” — verified paths and the plan→execute→feedback synthesis.
  • Ch. 7 autopsy + Ch. 8’s Figure 8-3 — premature closure at InfoGain 0.03, then the sub-2-second, ~$0.002 pipeline all eight pillars produce.

The one-sentence version: agents fail on representation, not intelligence — a graph of what the system knows, a graph of how it acts, a harness that remembers both, and the five flaws close one pillar at a time. Blueprint above; build is GraphOps; the rest, as the authors say, is engineering.
